items.title: Tim Willits doesn't think Rideshare's generative AI is damaging Saber's reputation
items.author: Julian Benson
items.summary: A few weeks ago, when I spoke with Tim Willits, chief creative officer at Saber Interactive, makers of games like Space Marine 2, SnowRunner, and World War Z,
items.text:
A few weeks ago, when I spoke with Tim Willits, chief creative officer at Saber Interactive, makers of games like Space Marine 2, SnowRunner, and World War Z, the company was dealing with the shitstorm that ensued from their announcement of Rideshare Stimulator.

The game's basically an Uber simulator, with you driving a car around town picking up fares, but Saber drew all kinds of bad attention when a former writer on the game revealed the game featured generative AI (something left undisclosed on the game's Steam page until recently) and CEO Matt Karch responded by attacking the writer in statements to the press. Something he has since apologised for.

So, naturally, we talked about generative AI and the reputational damage – or lack of – when getting caught out using it.

Watch on YouTube

Rideshare will have a main narrative, similar to other simulator games, in which you start your business in a city and grow it up as you complete jobs. Similar to something you would play through in Snowrunner. "All that is written by humans, all the missions are written by humans," Willits tells me. Where the generative AI appears is in Rideshare's Free Ride mode.

In Free Ride, when you pick up a fare, their dialogue will be generated using an LLM. "What we want to do is feed current events, like maybe there's some soccer game, and some ride will get in and talk about it," Willits explains. He says Saber are "using it here in a small part of a small game to test the waters." and that the company are "interested in how AI can help in games."

Willits says Rideshare is the only game in which Saber are using generative AI – "We don't have AI in Space Marine. We don't have AI in Hellraiser. We don't have AI in Jurassic Park, but we want to figure it out and we want to try something."

When I spoke with Willits, the thing I most wanted to know was why there was no AI disclosure on the Rideshare's Steam page when it was first revealed. Valve have a clear policy on disclosing the use of generative AI both in the production of a game and if any feature of the game makes ongoing calls to LLMs.

The reason, Willits says, is they "had an announce plan, but that got a little sideways". There was going to be a sneak peak, then there would have been reveals of the game's features in the future, and as part of that the generative technology would have been revealed. To indicate how early in the game's reveal rollout they are, Willits points out Rideshare's "not here" at Gamescom. "Unfortunately, we had some people talk about the game when they weren't supposed to be talking about the game and that just kind of escalated."

Though, I bring it back to Valve's AI disclosure policy because it doesn't make a distinction between whether a feature has been announced or not, only whether the technology is used in a game. Shouldn't the disclosure still have been there when the game was announced? "Okay, sure," Willits says.

The point I'm building to with Willits is that by not initially disclosing the use of AI, it seeds doubt about generative AI's use in Saber's other games. The tool may have been used but the company is not yet ready to announce or reveal it. I point to another of Saber's games, Road Kings, a new American trucking simulator which I really enjoyed at a preview event in April. While on the road, other drivers or job brokers may message you to ask for help, spurring an emergent quest. Certainly, there's no suggestion that these quests are generated by AI, but to a player the two systems could appear similar and they may now question 'Is this generative AI Saber's not copped to yet?'. "You may be overthinking it a little bit," Willits says. "I wouldn't worry about that. Again, the wishlists are up, interest is up, preorders across our games are up."

I didn't want to move on immediately, as Road Kings captures the issue well. I saw the game back in April but its embargo for the preview only came up after the Rideshare story had broken. I played and enjoyed that game and its mix of American Truck Simulator-style hauling blended with scenes you might see in a disaster move like Twister. But the comments on the preview were largely about the Rideshare news and Saber's use of AI. Willits, again, disagrees this is an issue. "I wouldn't really worry about that," he says. "The games will speak for themselves. You enjoyed Road Kings. The people that play it, they will enjoy it. I've been in the industry for 30 whatever years, you will always get crazy comments."

Willits points back to when he was working at id and they announced Quake 3 would need a video card to play. "We were roasted," he says. "The internet hate was crazy. 'You're ruining the industry. How can you make me pay $100 for a video card?' – imagine a $100 video card! – But the game came out and people liked it."

Willits also points to the launch of Steam, which, while a well-regarded platform now, was not universally loved at launch. In part because its servers struggled and its online functionality demanded more from peoples' internet than a lot of dial up and early broadband connections could provide. "I think we're in a period now of technology change that people are really unsure about," Willits says. "We, as game developers, don't really know what we're doing with it yet. Players don't really know what's going on with it. But I do think that there will be a game from somebody that will be so awesome that everyone will be like 'That's it. Now I get it.' I think the games will speak for themselves and when people play or they read your stories, and they watch the videos and they see the content, they will make their own determination."

As I've said in the past to other developers, I can believe there are ways these new AI technologies could benefit my work. For instance, the first transcription pass of most my interviews is done automatically because I use Google's Recorder app. But I also know the worst thing I could do with [insert AI tool of your choice] would be to generate an article for RPS. No one comes to this site to see something cobbled together by an LLM, they want something lovingly stitched together by these dyslexic typo-spewing hands. So I ask Willits what he thinks the benefit for Saber will be.

"As a game developer, if you're going to try something with brand new generative AI, it's much better to try it with something small [rather] than your biggest title," Willits says. "For us, part of our strategy at Saber is to make our mega hits – Space Marine 3, Jurassic Park, Turok – but we have to have smaller games that are consistent when it comes to how long it takes to make, how much money they make, [that's where] we experiment with things. Look at Spintires. That was an experiment that turned into a mega franchise. Rideshare fits into that category. It is a Rideshare simulator, where you drive around and you pick people up. There's really not much more you can really do there. And so for us, we wanted to be like 'Well, let's try this. Let's try it here because if it doesn't work out, it's on that game. It's not on our mega hits.'"

In the case of Rideshare's Free Ride mode, Willits says "This is a gameplay feature that is not possible without this technology. It would be logistically too hard, it'd be so expensive. We'd have to have an army." And, as he's described it, a mode where passenger dialogue is generated in response to current events fed into the game, I agree. Either you would have a madlibs style system of words being swapped in and out of repeating schemas, or a human writer adding additional lines in response to real world news events.

I do want to see if Saber are able to produce anything better than the other games that have stuck LLMs inside the throats of their characters. In Where Winds Meet, players quickly convinced one of the NPCs that they were pregnant, and another to provide cooking advice for potatoes and ketchup. That implementation and others were panned by developers Samuel Horti spoke to back in December.

My experience of generative AI dialogue has largely been formulaic and predictable. Which, could make for incredibly dreary car journeys. Ironically, the last taxi ride I was in I told the driver he was taking us to an engagement meal and he told me how AI was going to destroy the world by 2030.

Travel and accommodation to Gamescom was provided by the conference organisers.

items.title: 9 Sci-Fi Video Games So Good, Hollywood Needs to Adapt Them Now
items.author: Eddie Possehl
items.summary:
Published Sep 20, 2026, 6:01 AM EDT

Eddie Possehl is a dynamic and driven writer/director with a passion for the written word and all things film, television,
items.text:
Published Sep 20, 2026, 6:01 AM EDT

Eddie Possehl is a dynamic and driven writer/director with a passion for the written word and all things film, television, comics, and games. His passion for storytelling led him to establish his own production company in hopes of achieving his dreams.
His dedication to his craft has attracted renowned talent like Yuri Lowenthal to collaborate with him on his projects. As he grows and improves, Eddie is a shining example of a self-starter.

Science fiction video games have always been some of the most popular in the medium, and for very good reason. The worlds they bring to life and let players explore are gorgeous, intriguing, and epic. The characters within said worlds can be truly unique and great, especially when they're characters that the player genuinely enjoys controlling. Not to mention, they can also make good movie and/or television adaptations.

Adapting a video game franchise to film or television is quite difficult and doesn't always end up well — some may say that it's just not possible. This has led to a very understandable stigma, with people pretty much begging film studios not to adapt more video games. However, there are some video games out there that genuinely — if done right — could make for some awesome television or movie projects.

1
'Super Metroid' (1994)

Image via Nintendo

When it comes to the merging of Nintendo and sci-fi, it doesn't get much better than the likes of Super Metroid. The story is simply masterful, following this team as they slowly fall to... well, the fall of Reach. The characters at play are excellent and have a plethora of depth — not just being random super soldiers for the audience to watch aura farm — and would make incredible protagonists for a project outside of gaming. Plus, Halo could use a win after the conflicting feedback on their television series.

7
'Dead Space' (2008)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/dead-space-1.avif?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
Image via EA Redwood Shores

Combining genres is always fun when making content, because it allows the creatives behind said projects to really get experimenting with how to execute their stories and worlds. One of the best examples in gaming is the one and only Dead Space, a 2008 horror sci-fi game from Electronic Arts (EA).

Dead Space became a very popular franchise because of how well it blends these two genres, using the wacky, out-of-this-world style that comes with sci-fi to craft unique horror elements for players. While there have been some gigantic hits over the years, like the Alien franchise, the world could definitely use some more sci-fi horror, and the perfect place to find it is in the world of Dead Space.

8
'Mass Effect 2' (2010)

The Mass Effect franchise is one of the most popular sci-fi game franchises of all time, and for very good reason. The stories present in these games are exceptionally well-written, with some of the best characterization out there. Yes, the plot is amazing, but these characters are so great in almost every way, and there's no Mass Effect game where this is more true than the sequel, Mass Effect 2.

What makes this sequel the best is that it decides not to go into a full-force space opera — intergalactic battles with massive spectacle — and rather opts to give players a far more intimate and grounded story. This makes the story beyond emotionally compelling and honestly perfect for a film or series adaptation.

While there was an adaptation announced back in 2013, it's been in "development hell" ever since. So, until there's any true confirmation that something is actually moving forward, there may as well not be one in production.

Portal 2 has become a genuine pillar of gaming, and people want to see a Portal film. Recently, Backrooms director Kane Parsons said he would love to do one, and that has people begging for it. Of all the beloved sci-fi movies from the 1980s, few have proven more enduring than Ghostbusters. Four decades later, the ghoul-catching franchise is returning for more. Ghostbusters: Night Shift, as announced at the Annecy International Animation Film Festival, will make its big Netflix splash in 2027. In reference to the events of 1989's Ghostbusters 2, Ghostbusters: Night Shift is said to take place in 1994, "five years after the Ghostbusters took the Statue of Liberty for a walk."

Ben Hibon, Elliott Kalan, Jason Reitman, Gil Kenan, Amie Karp, and Dan Aykroyd will executive produce Ghostbusters: Night Shift. This animated rendition of the sci-fi juggernaut isn't the first of its kind. Back in the 1980s and 1990s, The Real Ghostbusters and Extreme Ghostbusters proved favorites of young audiences. But for every great (or not so great) entry into the Ghostbusters franchise, nothing can really compare to the original. The story of Peter (Bill Murray), Egon (Harold Ramis), and Ray (Aykroyd), as they are fired from Columbia University and eventually join forces with Winston (Ernie Hudson), is the stuff of cinematic legend.

Released in June 1984, Ghostbusters was a huge hit with critics upon release, with most of the praise going to the film's comedy, horror, and special effects. After admitting that the film is a clash of approaches that normally wouldn't work, critic Roger Ebert admitted that this blockbuster was the exception, writing, "It’s (1) a special-effects blockbuster, and (2) a sly dialogue movie, in which everybody talks to each other like smart graduate students who are in on the joke." Four decades on, the film is still a must-watch for all generations. However, you'll have to hurry, as Ghostbusters is being officially removed from the Netflix catalog starting October 1, 2026.

Which Sci-Fi Hero Are You Most Like?

How do you lead when the stakes couldn't be higher?

DI assess the threat, establish what needs doing, and get it done without waiting for permission.

What is your greatest strength in a crisis?

BImprovisation — I'm at my best when the plan falls apart and I have to invent a new one.

04

Who you are to others under pressure is who you really are.

How you respond when you're the only one who sees it defines everything.

DMy sense of safety — I know exactly what's out there now, and I can't pretend otherwise.

Your Sci-Fi Hero Is…

Your answers point to the iconic sci-fi hero who shares your instincts, your values, and your particular way of facing the impossible.

Arrakis · Dune

Paul Atreides

You carry a weight most people would crumble under — the knowledge of what you're capable of, and the burden of what you might have to become.

You see further ahead than others and you plan accordingly, even when the vision frightens you.

You are driven by loyalty to your people and a sense of destiny you didn't ask for but can't escape.

Paul Atreides is not simply a hero — he is someone who understands the cost of power and chooses to bear it anyway.

That gravity, that willingness to carry what others won't, is exactly you.

USS Enterprise · Star Trek

Captain Kirk

You lead with instinct, warmth, and an absolute refusal to accept a no-win scenario — because you've always believed there's a third option nobody else has thought of yet.

You take the mission seriously without ever taking yourself too seriously.

Your crew would follow you anywhere, not because you demand it, but because you've earned it.

That combination of warmth, audacity, and relentless optimism is unmistakably yours.

Princess Leia

You are the kind of person who holds the line when everyone else is losing faith — not because you're fearless, but because giving up simply isn't something you're capable of.

You lead through conviction. Your voice carries because your belief is unshakeable.

You gave up everything ordinary the moment you chose the cause, and you've never looked back.

Leia is not a supporting character in her own story — she is the moral centre of the entire rebellion.

That same fierce, principled, unbreakable core is what defines you.

Ellen Ripley

You are not reckless, not grandiose, and not particularly interested in being anyone's hero — you just refuse to stop when it matters.

You see threats clearly, you document the truth even when no one listens, and when the time comes you handle it yourself.

Ripley's heroism is earned, not performed. She doesn't have a speech — she has a flamethrower and a plan.

You share her composure under the worst possible pressure, and her refusal to pretend the monster isn't there.

When it counts, you don't flinch. That's everything.

Max Rockatansky

You have been through fire that would break most people — and what came out the other side is something the world underestimates at its peril.

You don't ask for help, don't need validation, and don't wait for anyone to tell you the rules no longer apply.

Your loyalty, when it finally arrives, is absolute — but it's earned in silence and tested in action, not in words.

Max is not a nihilist. He is someone who lost everything and found, against his will, that he still has something worth protecting.

That bruised, stubborn, ultimately human core is exactly yours.

items.text:
Published Sep 20, 2026, 4:00 AM EDT

Sharmila is an engineer-turned-gaming hardware journalist and freelance contributor at ScreenRant who has been covering the gaming and tech industry since 2021. While she first built her expertise writing about video games, she has since pivoted towards gaming hardware, with a focus on PC components, peripherals, handhelds, and performance-driven tech. When she’s not testing gear or writing about the latest hardware trends, she can usually be found diving into competitive shooters or keeping up with the evolving esports scene.

The Legend of Zelda's Link took to the high seas in The Wind Waker, but he's never truly adopted the life of piracy. If he did, though, there’s a good chance his adventure would look something like a meeting between The Legend of Zelda and Assassin’s Creed 4: Black Flag.

This might seem like a pipe dream, but one new Steam game gets surprisingly close to delivering an amazing version of this combination. As ridiculous as the premise sounds on paper, you can now try a free demo to see for yourself if the unusual cocktail works.

Released on September 18 on Steam, Draco and the Seven Scales is an indie Metroidvania from developer Ice Goat Games that puts players in the role of a pirate captain who sets out on a journey to save his greatest treasure. But things get complicated quickly when dark magic and a deal with a kraken enter the picture.

Interestingly, the game lets you switch between two very different kinds of adventure. You can explore the world on foot, where you’ll find dungeons, enemies, puzzles, and items to collect. When you’re done with the land, you can climb aboard your ship and sail across the ocean, opening up different routes and discovering new areas along the way.

Like in The Legend of Zelda games, Draco and the Seven Scales features seven top-down dungeons, each filled with enemies, puzzles, and items, while the wider overworld gives you plenty of reasons to explore rather than simply following a straight path from one objective to another.

And once you set sail, you’ll see Black Flag comparison starting to make sense. It’s not just about jumping into a boat to get from one island to another—your ship is also an important part of the adventure. You can upgrade its capabilities and cannons as you progress, and battles with enemy ships will have you face off with Her Majesty’s Royal Armada, alongside other bosses and rivals.

Draco and the Seven Scales also has plenty of the old-school charm you’d expect from a game inspired by classic top-down adventures. The visuals embrace Game Boy-inspired pixel art, while the soundtrack is built around melodic shanties that change depending on the areas you’re exploring. There are a plethora of items to discover, some useful for combat and puzzles and others tied to activities such as fishing.

If you’re not sure whether this particular mix of dungeon crawling and pirate adventure is for you, there’s an easy way to find out. Draco and the Seven Scales has a free demo available on Steam, so you can try its combination of exploration, puzzles, and sailing before deciding whether you want the full game. If you end up liking the demo, you can purchase the full version on Steam for $15.99, with an introductory 10% discount bringing it down to $14.39 until October 2.

If you’ve been looking for something unusual to play—like something that captures the feel of a classic The Legend of Zelda-style adventure but swaps the usual fantasy setting for pirates and open seas—Draco and the Seven Scales brings that intriguing combination to life. The Steam demo costs nothing, so there isn’t much stopping you from taking the ship out for a spin.

items.text:
With the fall TV season getting underway, The A.V. Club‘s editor-in-chief Danette Chavez wants to know: What series—new or returning—are you most looking forward to?


As always, we invite you to contribute your own responses in the comments—and send in some prompts of your own! If you have a pop culture question you’d like us and fellow readers to answer, please email it to avqa@avclub.com.

East Of Eden (October 1, Netflix)


While The Grapes Of Wrath is the John Steinbeck novel that most people probably encountered in their high school literature courses, East Of Eden is, for my money, his best work. A sprawling, multi-generational tale about good, evil, and the choices we make between them, it’s one part Biblical allegory and one part devastating exploration of the human condition. (Seriously, if you have never read it, please fix your life.) Do I think that a seven-part Netflix adaptation can successfully contain all those multitudes? I’m not sure, but I’m intrigued enough to find out. Particularly since it stars Florence Pugh and will clearly focus heavily on Cathy Ames, infamous antiheroine and the subject of endless debate among readers and literary critics about the nature of evil. To steal an idea from Steinbeck himself: It doesn’t have to be perfect; it just has to be good. [Lacy Baugher Milas]

Carrie (October 7, Prime Video)


I’m hot and cold on Mike Flanagan. I love Hush and enjoyed his first Stephen King adaptation, Gerald’s Game. Even Dr. Sleep and Ouija: Origin Of Evil punch well above their weight. Still, the hardlines, pastel covers, and whispered performances of Hill House lost me. I skipped his Netflix era along with The Life Of Chuck, because “From the hearts and minds of Stephen King and Mike Flanagan” is a tagline that causes me to die of cringe. Chuck notwithstanding, I tend to enjoy Flanagan’s King adaptations, so his Carrie show has my attention. That’s a story that feels incredibly salient for the social media age, when teen humiliation can be live-streamed for all the world to see. Sure, an eight-episode limited series is a long time to wait for a predetermined promposal. But maybe it’ll make the pig’s blood taste all the sweeter. [Matt Schimkowitz]

Cupertino (October 8, CBS)


We’re all understandably sick of seeing real and fictional tech billionaires and AI advocates champion their nefarious agendas, so I’m most curious to see how Cupertino positions itself in this sphere. I loved co-creators Robert and Michelle King’s most recent series, Evil, and they’re clearly good at making legal dramas work, as seen with The Good Wife universe. So I have faith in them to make, at the very least, an amusing broadcast drama that I can get hooked on again. Cupertino centers on two recently fired attorneys (played by Mike Colter and Rachel Keller) who start their own firm, mainly taking on clients aiming to fight back against the Goliaths controlling Silicon Valley. I’m intrigued by both the concept and the ensemble, which includes Nik Dodani, Busy Phillips, Renée Elise Goldsberry, and Ella Stiller. [Saloni Gajjar]

The Lowdown season two (October 14, FX)


The pleasures of The Lowdown are as straightforward as they are abundant: Great premise (amiable dramedy in the vein of Lodge 49 and Terriers that chooses the journey over the destination), great cast (Ethan Hawke, Keith David, Kaniehtiio Horn, and

Ryan Kiera Armstrong are back for season two, and are joined by Betty Gilpin and Tommy Lee Jones), and a setting that grows richer by the episode (Tulsa, OK). Even if series creator Sterlin Harjo hadn’t set up another uniquely compelling mystery in the upcoming season, I’d tune in to see Hawke as Lee Raybon, a character that lets the actor continue to show off his limitless range while also being of a piece with the other searching types in his repertoire. And did I mention Betty Gilpin is in the new season?? [Danette Chavez]

VisionQuest (October 14, Disney+)


As someone who liked WandaVision about 10 percent less than everybody I know—at least, once it stopped doing the fun TV pastiche stuff, and started defaulting to serving up cross-stitch material about grief—I was a little leery about next month’s Disney+ series VisionQuest. But I can’t say they didn’t get me: The show’s trailer, rolled out at D23 last month, really sold how fun the show could be, getting James Spader’s Ultron to Blacklist his way around an imaginary house while annoying the crap out of Paul Bettany’s NuVision. I’m not sold on the wider WandaVision family material the show is clearly building toward—it also turned me off of Agatha All Along—but I’m excited to at least watch the experiment play out for a few episodes, before wider franchise obligations inevitably win out. [William Hughes]

Crystal Lake (October 15, Peacock)


As an unreasonable slasher nut, I was skeptical about a prequel series centered on Friday The 13th‘s matriarch supreme, Pamela Voorhees. The first Friday essentially covers everything we need to know about the Voorhees family’s initially tragic, subsequently horrific descent into mayhem: Little Jason disappears in the lake, Pam cracks up, and horny camp counselors get iced in all sorts of inventive ways. What else did we need to know? While I’m anticipating (maybe dreading) some creative lore expansion from A24’s Peacock series, seeing Linda Cardellini decked out in Pam’s ’70s flannel and noting showrunner Brad Caleb Kane’s impressive résumé—including Lodge 49, Fringe, and It: Welcome to Derry—has me feeling cautiously optimistic about Crystal Lake. Frankly, seeing Cardellini cut loose on her victims with edged and serrated weapons is too much fun for even this wary horror hound to pass up. [Jarrod Jones]

The Fall And Rise Of Reggie Dinkins season two (November 2, NBC)


Okay, this is a little predictable, since I’m reviewing this Tracy Morgan-Daniel Radcliffe sitcom and all. But damned if I can’t wait to see how creators Robert Carlock and Daniel Means (alongside other Tina Fey sitcom factor hands like Phil Augusta, Meredith Scardino, and more) further expand the show’s fruitful comedic sandlot of fame, football and family. Morgan and Radcliffe have crafted an unexpected but hilariously lived-in odd couple energy as disgraced former NFL running back Reggie Dinkins and disgraced former indie film darling Arthur Tobin. And Erika Alexander, playing the seemingly thankless role of Reggie’s ambitious ex-wife and the only grownup in the room, is equally funny and human. The first season’s brisk 10-episode order saw the show sprint past plenty of scenarios and character dynamics the upcoming second outing can explore, and the show’s nimble handling of the hot button issue of gambling in American sports is only going to give the absurdly talented ensemble and writers more room to maneuver. [Dennis Perkins]

Black Doves season two (November 5, Netflix)


Black Doves was a perfect holiday binge with my parents: sleek, smart, twisty, and filled with charming British banter. We’d already been hooked on Slow Horses and this is that spy show’s shadier, more interpersonally tangled cousin. Erring towards Tom Clancy rather than James Bond, the middlebrow espionage has a brutal streak, which added an enjoyable edge to the otherwise comforting series of double-crosses. I’m happy to make this an annual tradition for as long as Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw want to get up to a little wetwork, and as long as they want to spar with Sarah Lancashire over who’s really in control. Add in a few new guest stars, another organization-spanning caper, and, as the British say, I’m sat. [Jacob Oller]

Yellowjackets season four (November 20, Showtime)


With all due respect to The Gilded Age (which returns on November 1), there is no premiere this season that matches my enthusiasm for the return of Yellowjackets. This is not because I have lofty expectations of this season, but because season three was so nuts that I have been waiting for 18 months just to see how the hell they’re going to wrap it up. And while I did enjoy season three largely for its camp factor (compared to its first season, which was more successful as a straightforward thriller), the fact that Yellowjackets‘ fourth and final season sees the girls return to their high school in New Jersey should help to avoid some of the wheel-spinning that befell the show’s last outing. Given that the creator Ashley Lyle and Bart Nickerson already said they planned to pick up the pace this time around, I’m looking forward to seeing something crazy. [Drew Gillis]

Dig (November 23, Peacock)


Digging! Everybody’s trying it this fall, whether it’s Tom Cruise doing Kirkland Signature Dr. Strangelove in Digger, or the Parks And Recreation duo of Amy Poehler and Michael Schur in their new Peacock comedy about archaeologists who stumble upon a potentially earthshattering secret while sifting through the ruins of ancient Greece. I know nothing of the source material—the novel Excavations by real-life archaeologist Kate Myers—but I have immense faith in the creative team here, which includes Schur’s wife, Single Parents co-creator and New Girl veteran J.J. Philbin. I’ve been eager to see Geraldine Viswanathan (who’s onboard as one of Poehler’s fellow archaeologists here) back on a TV comedy, and could Hugh Laurie be any better suited for a role than that of the hidebound professor leading the titular dig, someone I’m sure will have a totally measured and not at all explosive reaction to whatever artifact of inciting incident that his colleagues pull out of the ground? Here’s hoping they dredge up a trove of laughs along with it—if not, there’s always two seasons of Digman! to fall back on. [Erik Adams]


Dig (Image: Peacock)

items.text:
The European Commission proposed new rules around how under-15s access the likes of social media, AI chatbots, and online video games earlier this week. The draft legislation is called the EU Kids Act and calls for the setting up of a tiered system governing the types of accounts children under 15 can create to access such services, enforced by mandatory age verification for all users.

The documents laying out the proposal have been officially released, and based on the current wording the Commission have used to define what they class as an online game, it seems single player games that rely on online platforms like Steam for updates, distribution, or even a one-time authentication could be caught in the crossfire. That is, unless the definition is tightened up before the law is set in stone, if it indeed it makes it that far.

When the proposal originally leaked, prior to its official unveiling by European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, reports suggested there was no detail as to how the body had defined the concept of "online games" - and by extension, which sorts of games would fall under the proposed regulations. Now it looks as if that definition is rather broad, as it stands.

For instance, in a press conference held by the Stop Killing Games campaign about the proposed act, European Pirate Party senior policy adviser Paul Diegel - who serves as an assistant to sitting European Parliament member Markéta Gregorová - noted that the current draft of the legislation would even see single player games affected "because they're connected to Steam for updates". Since the proposal docs are publicly available via the European Commission's site, I've dug out the current version of the section on what is or isn't an online game as far as the proposed act is concerned. It reads as follows:

Video games have become an important part of the digital environment in which minors participate and interact with others, in a playful, goal-oriented or entertaining manner. Certain video gaming platforms allow the dissemination and exchange of user-generated content to an indeterminate number of recipients of the service and the facilitation of contact between these recipients. Such online games fall within the definition of online platforms referred to in Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 and should be covered by the scope of this Regulation.

At the same time, some online games that do not allow the dissemination of information to an indeterminate number of recipients should also fall within the scope of this Regulation. This is the case of any game that can be played on a computer, a mobile device, or a games console, irrespective of whether the game underlying software is subsequently executed locally, remotely, such as by means of durable medium, and irrespective of whether the service is provided free of charge, against payment, or against hybrid remuneration involving in-service (or in-application) purchases.

Online games that are accessible or purchasable exclusively through physical media, without any online component enabling their access, distribution, or purchase, are not considered online games for the purposes of this Regulation. For the avoidance of doubt, where an online game also has certain features corresponding to a video sharing platform, it shall be considered an online game for the purpose of this Regulation.

If I'm reading that right, the sole exception in the current proposal applies to games that can only be bought or accessed physically, not via an online storefront like Steam. Even if the online element's only being used to distribute the game and subsequently ship updates to it, it seems like it would fall under the purview of the regulation as it's written at this stage, meaning it'd be subject to age verification.

It's worth noting that the EU Kids Act is still just a proposal at the moment. Tightening up or refining definitions such as this one, so that the law only affects exactly the sorts of games it intends to, is something I'd peg as almost certain to happen as the pending legislation is revised and scrutinised as part of the EU's lawmaking process. That means that if the Act does eventually end up being set into law, it could have a definition that only singles out specific types of online game that mirror social media, in the sense of connecting children to endless other players they can chat with or see the user-created content of.

For now, I'm gonna go and spend what remains of my Friday afternoon writing about a topic less heavy on legal jargon.

items.title: Control Resonant review: A superbly strange action-RPG that'll make you feel tiny and godly at once
items.author: James Archer
items.summary:
Control Resonant's roaring melee battles and grasp of cosmic weirdness put this unlikely sequel up there with Remedy’s finest work.

Developer: Remedy
items.text:
Control Resonant's roaring melee battles and grasp of cosmic weirdness put this unlikely sequel up there with Remedy’s finest work.

Developer: Remedy Entertainment

Publishers: Remedy Entertainment

Release: September 24th 2026

On: Windows

From: Steam, Epic Games Store

Price: $60 / £50 / €60

Reviewed on: AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, 32GB RAM, Nvidia RTX 5080, Windows 11

Control Resonant review

Control Resonant, much like the inside-out, interdimensional cryptids it has you bashing with a shapeshifting stick, probably shouldn’t exist. At least not in the risk-averse, pennypinching reality that sometimes seems to have enveloped the art of gamesmaking, and that may have installed some scepticism into my own head. The sequel to a liked yet slow-selling shooter, which replaces both the original’s player character and its instantly recognisable, bureauca-brutalist setting, while violently pirouetting into open-world RPG melee brawling. Five words that Remedy, in all their thirty years of existence, have never previously let pass their lips.

But exist it does, which is fortunate, because the gamble pays off spectacularly. Resonant’s reality-bending trip across a kaleidoscopic Manhattan is as rich in stark views, eerie atmosphere, and creative quests as Control’s Oldest House ever was, driven along by strong character-first storytelling and Remedy’s best action in ages.

There is a lot of that action, so it seems like a good place to start. Control Resonant makes big changes on both sides of its fights, starting with the fact you are now Dylan Faden, brother and formerly brainwashed foe to Control’s Jesse. A sort-of free man for the first time in decades, Dylan takes to heroics with a weary but honest determination, fueled by the combined guilt over his prior bodypuppet misdeeds and concern for his now-missing sibling. Who, at least, grants him a parting gift of the Aberrant, which looks like it came from the same transforming amarments factory as Jesse's Service Weapon - just for swinging rather than shooting. Meanwhile, the people-warping Hiss and Mold are back as the main opponents, but in a positive departure, the enemy line-up is heavier on properly twisted, otherworldly foes than simple humanoids. Think floating, fuzzy megaspores, towering armless lumps with spikes for faces, and on several occasions, possessed buses. Mamdani’s New York, eh.

Mathematically, combat starts simple. Each Aberrant form - i.e., your weapons - gets its own button and a three-hit combo. Primary and secondary forms have three choices each, a kind of Whacking Things Greatest Hits of hammers, scythes, and nunchuks, plus your pick of a distinct combo finisher.

Pick up the cadence of these one-against-all battles, though – and factor in the active combat abilities you earn through boss victories – and Resonant’s melee starts clicking. And expanding. And exploding. Encounters are relentless, a barrage of enemy attacks matched only by Dylan’s own supernatural damage dealing, both parties busting their moves in storms of sparks, debris, and extradimensional haze. Aberrant hits and power deployments flow into each other beautifully, and even without engaging the manual lock-on, the game is uncannily good at interpreting which foe you’re trying to strike, so there’s little cause for frustration as you rapidly flick between opponents.

After a few upgrades, it’s possible to craft reliable stance break builds, particularly through combinations of the status effects that certain abilities specialise in. This can then turn Resonant’s already-satisfying slugging matches into something that resembles Doom Eternal as much as Devil May Cry, Dylan whooshing around arenas to chain together executions (themselves as gratifyingly animated as Doom’s) and snowball off their strength, healing, and poise damage buffs.

I still think the original Control’s combat is better than it’s sometimes described, especially if you invest in furniture-throwing, but it simply isn’t as dynamic or aggressive as this. Parrying? Never heard of it – Dylan has a dodge, but the skill tree tunes even that to serve as a proactive attack-boosting tool, rather than just a means of avoiding harm. Resonant wants its players to push. Begs for it, practically, and nearly thirty hours in, I’m still happy to oblige.

Difficulty-wise, Control Resonant is no Sekiro, though it can get tricky in its larger-scale fights (or if you neglect to keep the Aberrant fed with upgrades). However, it also has an impressively granular Assists menu, where you can customise individual combat aspects, down to minutiae like enemy projectile speed and perfect dodge window length. Some of these adjust both ways too, so you can crank up the challenge if desired.

The only places where Remedy’s character action inexperience peeps through are the boss battles. Some genuinely are enjoyable, one-on-one paranatural duels, though others are overly simple, their sense of threat owed to massive health bars and the sheer damage of their attacks – not the challenge of recognising and avoiding them. They do all have the striking and memorable visual design you’d want from an action-RPG boss, at least, and their reward of potentially build-altering new combat powers meant I never felt I was wasting my time going after them.

Resonant is also smart in how it handles upgrades and levelling up more generally. Spending points and materials on a single Aberrant form will buff the base damage and falter build-up for all forms, so while resources are scarce enough that you’ll still need to make decisions on which to prioritise – I, for one, fell in love with the clanking, stunlocking, poise-evaporating power of the secondary Drill form – you’re still incentivised to spend leftovers on less favoured weapons. This, simultaneously, keeps them at least fairly viable later in the game, so power doesn’t come at the cost of flexibility.

Dylan’s own talent tree also has, unusually, a geographical element. Beating enemies and completing side missions in one of Manhattan’s various sub-areas will essentially level up the area itself, improving drop rates, healing item potency, and the stock of the local resource vendor. It’s only with each new area level that Dylan himself gets a skill point to put into his tree (which, for the record, is bigger than chuffin' Yggdrasil). Defeating that region’s boss also 'resets' the area, respawning and toughening up roaming enemies in exchange for a fresh set of XP-bountiful side activities.

It’s a peculiar mechanism, but again, one that works. Tying power progression to time and effort spent in different areas motivates exploration, arguably more so than simply slathering the map in question marks, and in my mind created a tidy, almost Elden Ring-like loop of 'Get rewards, challenge boss, get rewards.' Lending, in turn, a more tangible and digestible structure to the open world.

That’s an open world, by the way, that absolutely stands up as a successor to the Oldest House. Not that some concrete-walled cameos are any less welcome, but Resonant manages to spread the original’s New Weirdness wider without it getting thinner. There are still loads of flavoursome oddities painted into the city’s details: redacted files dropped by fleeing agents, billboards making less sense as the patterning around them worsens, disturbed objects falling in the ‘correct’ direction as Dylan uses gravity anomalies to walk on ceilings and walls – meaning a messy, inverted fight can send pallets of detritus shooting up into the air. Best of all are the sidequests, which tend to focus on the imaginatively bizarre Altered Items that have escaped the House’s containment cells. Calming a stressed lightbulb, or singing to a room of terrified dancers in ritualistic karaoke, can be both funny and a pleasant cooldown from the tautness of the combat.

It’s never wacky, mind. Resonant’s strangeness is just as often played for drama, and quite successfully, in terms of how often it makes Dylan – and perhaps all of humanity – feel like some kind of cosmic sand grain. Expeditions into massive, impossible spaces; a soundtrack that knows when to hype and when to haunt; lingering mysteries around the invading forces; they all conspire to stoke a lonely, forlorn chill. A fear, really, of the unknowable, and of how for all Dylan’s superhuman strength, he’s still just one bloke with a metal bar and bad memories of life as his employers’ teenage lab rat. Which is cool! Sometimes being reminded of how small you are is necessarily to reinforce the story’s extinction-level stakes, before you can whip out that scythe again and rage against the dying of the light.

It bears noting that amid this raging, Resonant remains focused on itself, which is to say it goes light on the Remedyverse crossover stuff. I haven’t checked off every sidequest yet but at least in the main story, there’s no fanfare moment where the outline of Alan Wake ghosts into view, no big Old Gods of Asgard musical number, etcetera. Which, given how shrewdly the overlaps were worked into Control, Alan Wake II, and especially the latter’s The Lake House DLC, is a minor shame. There is, at least, one tune-heavy sequence that plays like a calmer, nonviolent Ashtray Maze tribute, plus a liberal sprinkling of lyrical tracks elsewhere, so the series' banger credentials stay intact for now.

Instead, the story puts a redemption-seeking Dylan front and centre, anchored by relationships with the two women in his life. Jesse, who’s off on a mission of her own, co-stars in a series of interestingly novel flashback sequences, leaving handler Zoe as the more regular presence. Zoe communicates mainly in Firewatch-esque radio dialogue to which you pick responses on the fly, choosing to show anger, reservedness, or the Dylan Special: guilt. This is not a branching kind of RPG, but this extra dash of agency is a nice way of better aligning with your character’s thoughts and reactions than was true of the original Control. And the regularity of Zoe’s chats – which you can often instigate yourself – makes sure they stay effective, convincing building blocks for a blossoming friendship that may not otherwise have felt earned.

On the technical side, Resonant also looks the business, Remedy’s love for ray/path tracing and some of the less problematic DLSS tech being even more apparent here than in Alan Wake II. Its supposed Steam Deck support hasn’t quite panned out, however, with potato settings and heavy FSR upscaling failing to keep it above 30fps in busy city scenes. In truth, the whole thing could use another polish patch as well, as I’ve had a few instances of background music briefly cutting out, or enemies getting stuck on scenery. On one occasion I was slapped through a wall after biffing a dodge, which ironically progressed me slightly further through the mission, though less helpful was the bug that kept resetting my outfit choices when loading or fast-travelling to a certain region in the postgame.

I can forgive a few scuff marks, though, when they're acquired in the process of bold thinking and radical redesigning on this scale. That Remedy have realised this ambition with such rousing action, and a truly fresh take on one of the most well-trodden locales in games, is worthy of applause. Hopefully that this isn’t the last we see of the Faden twins, even if the next one is a cel-shaded fishing sim or something.

items.title: Dog in the Machine reinvents the domino tactics of Into The Breach as a mecha dog show, with players teaching their hounds tricks
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: If the organisers of Crufts ever have to produce a season of Robot Wars, the results probably won't be a million miles away from Dog in the Machine - a new
items.text:
If the organisers of Crufts ever have to produce a season of Robot Wars, the results probably won't be a million miles away from Dog in the Machine - a new turn-based tactics puzzler that's sort of Into The Breach but with a greater emphasis on props and tricks.

The story in brief: it's Future-O-Clock, and we humans all live in a whirring mecha-city, attended by our loyal mecha-dogs (it's not clear to me what's happened to actual, flesh-and-blood dogs - hopefully we haven't rendered them extinct through in-breeding, or slaughtered them to make lard). Except that oh blast, humans have just been exiled from the city, due to causes unknown.

In our absence, the city's infurnal cleaning bots are trying to break down all of our beloved labrobodoodles for parts. How pawful! Fortunately, the handsome electrohounds absolutely excel at teeing up domino-chain reactions on modestly sized grid maps. Here's a trailer.

Watch on YouTube

Developers Studio Chahut and publishers Goblinz Publishing have just reminded me that Dog in the Machine has a release date - 27th September. Thanks to that email, I became aware of Dog in the Machine's demo, which I have now played a little and enjoyed. In each level, you move your Autodog around to defeat a bunch of bots. You've got a limited energy supply to bestow on regular moves and repeatable "core" attacks, once-per-turn special abilities, and wildcard "tricks" such as duplicating the previous special ability, or "teleporting" by way of a tunnel.

Given that you're outnumbered, you've got to be efficient and preferably, turn enemies against each other. A simple strategy is using a charging bite to knock one foe into the path of another's attack. A more complex approach is to exploit terrain fixtures such as conveyor belts or impact-triggered laser defences. Very Into The Breachy, yes, though it's relatively relaxed, as you can undo moves without penalty, and it feels like there's a greater focus on the terrain fixtures. Some of the maps are like pinball machines, almost.

In addition to trashing the rampaging roombas, you've got to worry about an alarm bar gauge that ends the game once filled. Enemies add points to it, but you can remove those points by damaging and destroying them. It's a bit like the alert system in Invincible Inc, though it doesn't seem as elaborate.

I like the cartoon sci-fi aesthetics. It's all very colourful, clicky-clacky and burbly-whirry. I also like the idea that the whole thing is sort of an agility competition in disguise. items.title: TIFF 2026: Hombre Al Agua, Paradise Lost, Faith
items.author: Cortlyn Kelly
items.summary: In its 51st edition, the Toronto International Film Festival’s Special Presentation category comprises stories of complex parents, recentering their identity
items.text:
In its 51st edition, the Toronto International Film Festival’s Special Presentation category comprises stories of complex parents, recentering their identity as individuals. Interestingly, the focus on selfhood is overshadowed by a much broader conflict. Of these movies, it’s most peculiar how it explores motherhood versus fatherhood, emotionally and morally.

Set in rural, suspiciously tranquil Mexico, “Hombre Al Agua” gets gritty with its characters and their relationships. Parents and lovers, Juana (Esmeralda Pimentel) and Camilo (Gael García Bernal), don’t make much sense together, which becomes increasingly obvious as their paths of personal growth diverge throughout the film. As Camilo integrates into Juana’s family, working for her power-hungry father (Jorge Salinas), the more he loses his grasp on what’s right and what he should be true to.

To help the audience better understand this surrealist story, Bernal, who also wrote and directed the film, weaves in voiceover narration. Peppered with a nature-forward sound design, with the breeze blowing and birds chirping, we, too, are immersed in the countryside silence that Camilo and guests are acclimating to. The backdrop of their estate is beautiful but intentionally lacks that lived-in feeling. Everyone who stays there is untethered from their surroundings, blowing with the wind, leaving loose ends that are written off as fever dreams. “This is a thriller, not a melodrama,” a man utters to Camilo after he’s caught sneaking around their property, a meta proclamation of Bernal’s vision for his story.

Albeit scattered, “Hombre Al Agua” is weirdly entertaining. Each new idea is presented clearly, and most interestingly, the cultural and class themes give the movie more body than the simple character arcs at its center. Camilo’s Cuban heritage poses some political assumptions; the running joke about his radicalism due to his ethnicity highlights certain microaggressions with nuance. His career at his father-in-law’s factory is also compromised by his true beliefs, but he does his best to tread lightly as the tides shift. Bernal’s development of Camilo, behind and in front of the camera, is strongest, making the supporting characters feel like figments in the reality he’s trying to build.

Dissecting and dissolving grief is an endless experiment, certainly one of the most difficult matters for humans to digest. Yeon Sang-ho’s newest film, “Paradise Lost,” moves through multiple realities where a single mother navigates loss. Quaking with nuance that feels drawn from some variation of firsthand experience, “Paradise Lost” achieves a striking, gutting feeling because Yeon’s mother wrote it.

A lack often forces reflection or regret; what could have been done differently? What would one give to get their heart’s desires? These questions swirl at the film’s center. After So-young (Kim Hyun-joo) loses her son, Seon-wu (Bae Hyeon-seong), in a camping trip kidnapping along with 12 other kids, grief consumes her. After several years, an AI company, TransHuman, invents a virtual reality that recreates the lost children. This concept isn’t exactly original, but it’s eerily close to our current technological state. Shockingly, this anecdote is only a stepping stone to the film’s true conflict: Seon-wu resurfaces almost 10 years later.

Bae’s sinister performance chills every scene. At no point do we trust this older version of Seon-wu, but our faith in So-young’s morality deteriorates most after her son returns. Her inability to connect with her virtual or real son proves that these two beings (or entities) spiral into putting others in danger. Knowing the story is written by a mother-son duo provides some reasoning for the way the story unfolds and resolves, but there is a looming carelessness, an absence of logic.

However, the story’s subtlety and significance lie in how it positions single mothers as the most vulnerable. Other parents who lost their children began to move on from their virtually recreated children, relying on their partners and other children. For So-young, this was never an option, therefore catalyzing the audience’s (eventually limited) empathy for her.

Faith is more often than not associated with some form of religion; regardless, faith is rooted in a foundation at the intersection of trust and belief. Director Paul Andrew Williams titles his new film, “Faith,” after the concept, and puts his audience to the test till the very end.

Gina (Erin Doherty) is a single, spunky mum of an almost 10-year-old boy. She cares about him fearlessly, but that doesn’t dull her youthful nature; she plays trivia at the pub and craves a good hook-up every now and then. Enter Michael (James McAvoy), a mysterious new man at the bar, whose gentlemanly politeness squashes Gina’s hopes of a one-night stand. The two of them only ever simmer, keeping their distance until tragedy strikes.

Like the mother of “Paradise Lost,” Gina loses her only son, leaving her devastated and unable to function. In this state of grief, Doherty’s raw and unwavering performance creates unpolished conditions for how a grieving person treats those around them; misguided cruelty to those closest to you is easy to throw around in the wake of such pain. Michael remains patient with Gina, and McAvoy embodies this creepily kind demeanor with ease, a role he has often been cast in lately.

A memento of a bejeweled bird that Michael carries constantly in his pocket is the first symbol that spirituality is at play. In the most ghostly moments, the score haunts with humming vocals of a Sunday service. Every day is overcast in Gina’s small town, and this gloom, underscored by tolling bells, suggests that something unseen lurks and pulls secret strings. Williams lets Doherty carry the film’s deeper meaning by having her lean into cult-like behavior without question, but “Faith” ultimately misfires in its attempt to fictionalize religion’s real-world capacity to help people heal.

items.title: "We're trying to make it easier": Valve confirm the Steam Frame is just the start of plans to get Steam games working on compatibility-challenged ARM PCs
items.author: James Archer
items.summary: The Steam Frame, unfortunately RAM shortage-ravaged as it is, is unique among virtual reality headsets for its ability to run Steam games – VR or 'flat' alike
items.text:
The Steam Frame, unfortunately RAM shortage-ravaged as it is, is unique among virtual reality headsets for its ability to run Steam games – VR or 'flat' alike – entirely on its own, internal compute hardware. It is, in effect, a SteamOS PC for your face. Yet as I waxed about in our review, this feature’s impact could extend far beyond the Frame itself, as it’s based on new compatibility tech that Valve now hope to bring to a broader range of PCs and laptops. Potentially, according to staff speaking with RPS, making bonafide gaming systems out of previously unfriendly computers.

Explaining, I’m afraid, involves some gear jargon. Most PC games are exclusively made to run on processors built using the x86 architecture, the type used for all the mainstream Intel Core/AMD Ryzen chips we probably have inside our rigs right now – as well as in the Steam Deck and Steam Machine. Processors based on the rival ARM architecture, however, have become popular in non-gaming circles for their efficiency and battery life benefits to tablets and skinny laptops. These advantages convinced Valve to use an ARM chip for the Frame, but while a few hundred games know how to play friendly with the architecture, that’s well short of the thousands that Valve fancied to run locally on their new headset.

The solution was FEX, an open source x86-to-ARM emulator whose developers were approached by Valve and funded by them, on the sly, for years. Just as Proton makes Windows games compatible on the Linux-based SteamOS, FEX makes x86 games compatible on the ARM-based Frame, and its benefactors aren’t stopping there.

"Oh, for sure," Valve engineer Pierre-Loup Griffais replied when I asked if Valve are exploring game compatibility for other ARM PCs. "Yeah, I think one of the things that we want to do, and that the Frame is kind of paving the way for, is just more general SteamOS for ARM, right? There's a bunch of devices where you could have a great experience running SteamOS on there, that are currently kind of this adjacent ecosystem that's just a little bit different. But not really that different, in our opinion."

In theory, then, FEX could be deployed to make (at least the bulk of) Steam libraries playable on machines that currently struggle. Modern ultraportable laptops, 2-in-1s, and mini PCs included. Performance on integrated graphics would, uh, vary, and there might still be a significant barrier in the form of devicetrees: basically data-based maps that tell operating systems where to find all the different hardware components of an ARM chip. These layouts vary from manufacturer to manufacturer, so part of Valve’s work may involve digging up as much devicetree data as they can before FEX is put to work.

Regardless, they remain keen on the idea. "I think we want to enable all that stuff," Griffais continued. "And yeah, I think in general, ARM chips are more of a force that's coming on the PC side. There's a lot of laptops and even desktop-ish platforms that are in the pipe, and so we're interested in making sure people can have a good experience working through their whole library on there. And to not have a situation where... like, the worst case scenario would be 'Oh this device is good, and the specs are good, the value is good, but I have to leave a portion of my catalogue behind if I'm even considering it.'

"We don't like those kinds of choices, so we're trying to make it easier for those sorts of new devices to show their value instead of having to be evaluated on a different [game] library. Or compatibility tradeoffs in general."

Fellow Valve engie Josh Hudman also suggested that the company prefers to develop tech with multiple uses and applications, citing their work on TMR (Tunnel Magnetoresistance) thumbsticks that made it into both the Frame and the recent Steam Controller refresh. Some ideas, he claims, were even cut from the Frame as they weren’t perceived to be useful elsewhere.

"A lot of the technology we work on, we try to keep that in mind," Hudson said of Valve’s multifunction fixation. "When we do, like, thumbstick development, or wireless development, it's not necessarily, specifically focused on whether it's for VR hardware or whatever. It's more like, 'Is this technology going to make us better at developing future technologies? Does it improve the gaming experience? Is it just a general technology that's a good investment of time and energy?'

"And I think there's a lot of elements in the Frame, and our other hardware too, that we make that decision, and go after those technologies. Because there were some technologies we could have looked at on the Frame, which felt like they were very specific and didn't scale to other things. We try to focus more on the things that scale to other hardware, and our overall technology efforts."

As someone who’s long coveted the endurance of ARM-y Snapdragon laptops, but was never quite sure enough of their non-work abilities to pull the trigger on one, the prospect of an even more hardware-agnostic Steam feels very much 'for me.' More so than the ability to play Hades on a headset, at least. Obviously it’s all possiblies and potentials right now, but I can see Valve making the effort to see wider FEX support through, especially if the £889 / $1,059 Frame doesn’t do the numbers they’d like.

items.text:
Bill Gurley spent years on Wall Street, built his career as a partner at Benchmark, worked through Uber’s hypergrowth era, and now serves on the board of the Santa Fe Institute, where he studies complexity and systems thinking.

Featured clips

Obsessive Learning in Founders

The Craft of Storytelling and Writing

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript | X

In this episode, Bill shares the mental models he returns to most often, including systems thinking, second- and third-order effects, and the importance of understanding both the bedrock of your field and the bleeding edge.

He explains what separates great founders, why storytelling and product instincts matter, how he uses AI across different models, and what he sees coming in open source, China, stablecoins, tokenization, payments, and venture capital.

+ Check out Runnin’ Down a Dream: How to Thrive in a Career You Actually Love

++ Check out the Granola Notes

Tiny Lessons

Trajectory matters more than the starting place.

“Success requires balancing a deep knowledge of history with an obsessive focus on the technological edge where disruption happens.”

“I think more people would benefit by studying the history of whatever field they’re in.”

“If it’s tedious to learn, it isn’t a passion. I don’t think you’re in the right lane.”

“I think that anybody in any field should want to be curious about the bleeding edge and what happens.”

“You should understand the really old stuff, the history, because it’s differentiating and shows a passion and it gives you a great frame of mind, but you also want to really understand the new edge. If you do both of those things, I think you’re a power player in your field.”

“If you have to write it out and make it stand alone and be cogent, you’ll think through more of the problems and it’ll be more cohesive and you’ll figure out the loose ends and you’ll tie them up.”

“If regulation gets extremely difficult and mundane and expensive, that could actually lead to more oligopoly.”

“I would describe complex systems as multivariable nonlinear systems. And multivariable nonlinear systems are very hard to predict. They can behave one way for a long time, and then one variable can switch and they can behave another way—the weather, stock markets, all these things. There are consequences that can be first, second, or third-order. You can’t just think with a linear model or just think about one variable because things can go way off the path. You need to be aware that if you make a change here, it could change something here, which could change something there, and it has to be the whole system.”

“You’ve got to be really conscious of the consequence and not get too deterministic about a single metric or a single variable.”

“I’ve always thought of Wall Street as the buyer of the product that venture capitalists create because the eventual liquidity is either an M&A (merger and acquisition) or an IPO (initial public offering).”

One question to ask before hiring or investing in someone: Is this person going to do this no matter what?

items.text:
Mario Harik is the CEO of XPO, one of the largest logistics companies in the world.

For years, he was the protege of legendary entrepreneur Brad Jacobs (who built eight multibillion-dollar companies from scratch). Today, Mario leads 40,000 people with a management style shaped by what he learned. It’s a rare combination of smart capital allocation, discipline, deep listening, and a genuine belief in human potential.

Mario shares how he uses real-time data and second-order thinking to make better decisions faster, how he hires and develops A players (and the test that instantly tells you who isn’t one), how he runs meetings that pull the best thinking out of the most junior person in the room, what he learned working alongside one of the best entrepreneurs of our generation, and why ego, complacency, and small goals are quietly capping everything.

I hope you enjoy this conversation as much as I did.

Featured clips

Letting go of perfection and understanding how people operate

Learning from frontline employees and feedback loops

Analytical approach to risk and decision-making

Creating a high-performance environment through belief and feedback

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript

+ Check out the Granola notes.

Tiny Lessons

“If you set big goals, you achieve great things. If you set small goals, you achieve small things.”

“Ego is thinking you’re so good at something that you stop learning.”

“I worry if I’m in a team meeting and everybody’s aligned on a solution.”

In meetings, senior people speak last.

“A lot of leaders spend time on the output. You’ve got to spend time on the inputs.”

Tell people what to do but not how. When you tell them how, you set the ceiling at your best idea not theirs.

If somebody quits and your feeling is ‘whew, that’s good news’ — you should have gotten rid of them long ago.

“Most people think at the speed of speech. You can train your mind to go much faster.”

“When I give constructive feedback, I never make it subjective. I always ground it on data.”

“A lot of what people flag as potential issues ends up being why somebody fails at work.”

Yearly performance reviews are theater. “Performance reviews should be done on a daily and weekly basis.”

Don’t stop at the first answer. Double and triple-click.

The three variables that matter most when hiring: “Are they good at what they do? Are they serious about work? Are they kind?”

“It’s okay to have some friction.”

“Disagree all you want. Just focus on the problem, not the person.”

“Winning breeds winning.”

“Life is short. You’ve got to set big, big goals.”

“If you want to create alpha, don’t settle for a local maximum.”

“My hobbies are my work and my kids.”

“Every morning you have a choice: do the job the way you always do it, or learn new things.”

The only competition is yourself. “The bar isn’t beating the competition. The bar is: are we achieving the best we can achieve?”

“Work is part of life, the same way life is part of work.”

“When you show someone you believe in them, they have much higher odds of being great.”

“Every person in their own way is beautiful. Your job is to find how their mind works, not flatten it.”

“The biggest lever in business is who’s on the team and how they work with each other.”

items.text:
The anticuchos at Cholapink. | Cholapink

We’ve been covering various NYC restaurants, food, drinks, bars, etc. news intel over on our daily newsletter (please sign up if you haven’t already!), but we’re also making it easier for everyone to catch up by rounding ‘em up here every week (check out August, July, and June’s).

September 11

A new Peruvian spot from a chef and a rapper

Peruvian chef Jaime Pesaque (of notable Lima restaurant Mayta) and Puerto Rican rapper Daddy Yankee (yes) are teaming up to open a new fast-casual Peruvian restaurant in New York City this fall. Cholapink is opening at 32 Spring Street, near Mott Street, in Nolita in October. The menu highlights grilled street food, also known as anticuchos, with ajis (marinades and sauces) like miso-glazed chicken thighs, pineapple gochujang pork belly, yuzu-amarillo fish, and spicy peanut mushrooms.

An NYC taco fave gets private equity funding

NYC’s favorite taqueria chain Los Tacos No. 1 is getting investment money from private equity firm TSG Consumer Partners, as reported by QSR. After the news was announced, people took to commenting on Los Tacos’ Instagram page, worrying about potential quality issues and increased prices (see: the discourse about Salt Hank’s acquisition by food hall behemoth Wonder). The team responded, assuring that they’re “definitely not messing with the tacos,” and that the reason they took the investment is so that they can “keep getting better at it” and expand. The restaurant recently partnered with Gap on an apparel collaboration.

An NYC artist and restaurant owner has died

Lucien Smith, the NYC artist who had revived iconic Chinatown restaurant Food, has died at the age of 37, as reported by Cultured. The restaurant had posted last week that it was temporarily closing.

Fall restaurant season is HERE

Bad news: Summer is unofficially over. Good news: it’s fall preview season! Part one of Eater NY’s most anticipated restaurant openings of the fall is on the website; part two is over on Substack.

An anticipated Hong Kong-style diner finds its address

Turns out chef Lucas Sin is indeed opening his dream cha chaan teng Lok Kee at M Star Cafe in Chinatown, where he’d been popping up this late summer.

Mrs. and Mr. Swift’s NYC night out

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce dined at Ambassadors Clubhouse on Saturday, September 6, per a rep for the fancy Indian restaurant in Nomad. They dined in one of the private dining rooms, enjoying drinks and food. I’d bet they ordered the tableside whiskey cocktail, the Patiala Peg.

Top Chef winner pops up with bodega preview

Chef Danny Garcia continues previewing his forthcoming Latin halal restaurant, Only Goods, with a pop-up bodega this weekend. It’s taking place at 307 Bedford Avenue, near South Second Street in Williamsburg on Saturday, September 12, from 1 to 5 p.m.

A kaiseki anniversary party

Tribeca kaiseki Muku is celebrating its first anniversary with a special tasting menu this fall, featuring dishes like a rare Japanese sweetfish and harako meshi, a dish of white rice, salmon, and roe. The $375 menu is available through Saturday, October 3.

A 10-year-restaurant collab celebration

To celebrate Fish Cheek’s 10th birthday, the restaurant is teaming up with other NYC restaurants and bars for special collaboration dishes. Starting on Saturday, September 12, find the choo chee michelada and zapp popcorn chicken at Lower East Side cocktail bar Double Chicken Please; the razor clams with nam jim seafood at American Asian Hudson Square restaurant Kiko; the clam pie at both the East Village and Bushwick locations of Ops Pizza; and sliced flaky Thai coconut cake at sibling gluten-free Nolita bakery Bub’s. And then, starting on Monday, September 14, there’s a special burger at Prospect Heights Jewish bistro Gertrude’s.

September 4

A Vietnamese American bakery returns to Brooklyn

Some good news: After baker Doris Hồ-Kane shuttered her Vietnamese American bakery in February, she’s working on bringing back Bạn Bè to its original Carroll Gardens neighborhood.

Hồ-Kane launched a Kickstarter campaign to help fund the opening. She’s aiming to open in November at 115 Columbia Street, at Kane Street, in the Columbia Street Waterfront District.

The resurrected space will have a takeout window and a first-time indoor dine-in space. On deck are pastries and sweets like the beautiful bright-green pandan honeycomb cake and new stuff like pandan lime madeleines and pandan chocolate tiramisu. For savory vegeterian items, look for banh mi, Vietnamese crepes, and summer rolls, along with coffee and tea drinks.

The McNally son ventures into the restaurant world

Keith McNally’s son, George, opens his Tribeca restaurant, Faux, on Thursday, September 3, at 277 Church Street, between White and Franklin streets. McNally (the son) knows the restaurant life well, having worked at his father’s spots like Balthazar and the D.C. location of Minetta Tavern. Faux’s chef Kristina Ramos (who worked at Minetta in D.C.) is cooking up a coastal French menu, with highlights including broiled oysters and steak frites. The ground-floor restaurant includes a downstairs bar, Prevz, with late-night food and a bouncer. Book restaurant reservations on OpenTable.

Buy stellar baked goods for a good cause

Expert baker Natasha Pickowicz is hosting a community bake sale this weekend to raise money for Queens nonprofit Make the Road New York. Our Little Bake Sale features chefs like Pickowicz herself, Zoë Kanan of Elbow Bread, Morgan Knight of Saint Street Cakes, Flynn McCarry of Cove, Ali Domrongchai, and many others. It’s free to attend; each pastry is worth one ticket, which is $10. The event, which is a partnership with indie food publication Cake Zine, takes place on Sunday, September 6, from 3 to 5 p.m. at Little Island, the park on Pier 55 along Hudson River Park at West 13th Street.

Two NYC restaurants take over Times Square Red Lobster

A restaurant group behind NYC restaurants, including American brasserie the Smith and pizzeria Parla, is taking over the recently shuttered Red Lobster in Times Square, as reported by the New York Post. The business plans to open a fifth location of the Smith and a pizza-slice spinoff of Parla at a two-floor address at 582 Seventh Avenue, between West 41st and 42nd streets, set to debut in 2028.

A bread bakery grows in Crown Heights

In more bakery news, Apt. 2 Bread, a micro-bakery best known for its focaccia, is working on opening a bread-focused bakery named Boots Bread in Crown Heights. Carla Finley is teaming up with Megan Wang for the new venture. When the bakery opens, expect all sorts of breads made with regional grains.

What’s happening with Food?

Looks like Chinatown restaurant Food, the revitalized Chinatown restaurant now run by artist Lucien Smith, seems to have “closed until further notice,” per its Instagram.

A Radio Bakery branch is temporarily closed

The Greenpoint location of Radio Bakery is temporarily closing for renovations, from Tuesday, September 1, through Monday, September 21. To help ease the demand, the Prospect Heights location is staying open later (until 6 p.m.) through Sunday, September 13.

An Austin bar pop-up worth going to

One of my personal favorite bars ever, Austin’s Nickel City, is coming to New York City for a pop-up this month. Owner Travis Tober is taking over the bar of Romeo’s in the East Village, on Wednesday, September 9, from 8 to 11 p.m., with Dr Pepper Old Fashioneds, Mexican martinis, and more.

If you’re going to Harry Styles…

If your Labor Day weekend plans include seeing Harry Styles at Madison Square Garden this Friday, September 4, and/or Saturday, September 5, we’ve got a handy guide for you, at least when it comes to drinking and eating. Pro tip: Make sure you’re seated/standing by the time opener Jamie XX plays his final song, because Harry and company take the stage at the same time to kick off the show.
